parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think of the seven building blocks that all other units are made from - which items in the list are fundamental and cannot be broken down further, and which are combinations like charge or force?
parts.proper_answer: Underline electric current and time only.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the SI Base Family**
You have seven SI base quantities to learn by heart. The ones you meet most are mass, length, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature and amount of substance. Everything else is derived from them.

Step 2: **Sort the List**
Charge is $Q = It$, so it is current $\times$ time and is derived. Force is $F = ma$, so it is mass $\times$ length / time$^2$ and is derived. That leaves electric current with unit ampere $\text{A}$ and time with unit second $\text{s}$, both of which are base quantities.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: The full equation for distance is $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. Compare this with the shorter version given - what must be true about the starting speed $u$ for the first term to disappear?
Hint 2: All SUVAT equations only work in one special type of motion. What must be true about the size of $a$ through time, and about the shape of the path?
parts.proper_answer: 1. Initial velocity / speed is zero. 2. Acceleration is uniform / constant and motion is in a straight line.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why the $ut$ Term Is Missing**
The complete relation is $$s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$$ where $u$ is initial velocity. You are given only $$s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$$ This matches only if $$ut = 0$$ for all $t$, so $$u = 0$$ The object must start from rest.

Step 2: **Why Acceleration Must Be Constant**
This formula comes from integrating a constant acceleration, or from the area under a uniformly increasing velocity-time graph. If $a$ changed with time the $\tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ result would fail. So the second condition is that $a$ has constant non-zero magnitude and the motion stays along a straight line with no change of direction.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on how steep the line is at $t = 8.0\text{ s}$ compared with at $t = 14.0\text{ s}$, and whether the line is sloping uphill or downhill at each time.
Hint 2: Link steepness to size of acceleration and uphill versus downhill to sign of acceleration - how do the two times compare on both ideas?
parts.proper_answer: Magnitude at $t = 8.0\text{ s}$ is less than at $t = 14.0\text{ s}$. Direction at $t = 8.0\text{ s}$ is opposite to that at $t = 14.0\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read Steepness for Magnitude**
On a $v$-$t$ graph, a steeper slope means a larger magnitude of acceleration. Around $t = 8.0\text{ s}$ the line rises gently from $t = 4\text{ s}$ to $t = 12\text{ s}$. Around $t = 14.0\text{ s}$ the line falls much more steeply from $t = 12\text{ s}$ to $t = 16\text{ s}$. So the magnitude at $8.0\text{ s}$ is smaller.

Step 2: **Read Uphill Versus Downhill for Direction**
A rising $v$-$t$ line means positive acceleration, a falling line means negative acceleration, which is the opposite direction along the straight track. At $8.0\text{ s}$ the graph slopes up, at $14.0\text{ s}$ it slopes down. So the directions are opposite to each other.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
key_concepts: acceleration as gradient of v-t graph
hints: Hint 1: Look at the long straight section that passes through $t = 4.0\text{ s}$ from $t = 0$ to $t = 12\text{ s}$ - what does a straight $v$-$t$ line tell you about acceleration there, and which two easy-to-read points could you use?
Hint 2: Work out change in velocity divided by the time taken between two clear points, for example from $v = -10\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $v = +20\text{ m s}^{-1}$, and keep the unit $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use the Gradient Idea**
Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph: $$a = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$$ At $t = 4.0\text{ s}$ you are on the straight line from $t = 0$ to $t = 12\text{ s}$, so $a$ is constant there and any interval on that line will do.

Step 2: **Pick Clean Points and Calculate**
A common mistake is to use only $t = 4.0\text{ s}$. Instead use the whole straight section. For example from $(0, -10)$ to $(12, 20)$: $$a = \frac{20 - (-10)}{12 - 0} = \frac{30}{12}$$ $$a = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$$ The magnitude is $2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}$. Equivalently $(0-(-10))/4$ or $(20-0)/(12-4)$ gives the same result.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
key_concepts: displacement as area under v-t graph
hints: Hint 1: Remember that displacement is the net signed area between the graph and the time axis up to $t = 12.0\text{ s}$ - note that part of the graph from $t = 0$ to $t = 4.0\text{ s}$ lies below the axis.
Hint 2: Calculate the small triangle below the axis as negative and the large triangle above the axis as positive, then add them, or use $1/2 \times (20-10) \times 12$ for the net area.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Set Up Signed Areas**
Displacement is net area under the $v$-$t$ graph: $$\text{displacement} = \text{area above axis} - \text{area below axis}$$ From $t = 0$ to $4\text{ s}$ velocity is negative, forming a triangle of base $4\text{ s}$ and height $10\text{ m s}^{-1}$. From $t = 4\text{ s}$ to $12\text{ s}$ velocity is positive, forming a triangle of base $8\text{ s}$ and height $20\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Combine to Get Net Displacement**
Calculate: $$\text{area below} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 4 \times 10 = 20\text{ m}$$ $$\text{area above} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times (12-4) \times 20 = 80\text{ m}$$ $$\text{displacement} = 80 - 20 = 60\text{ m}$$ So the magnitude of displacement from X at $t = 12.0\text{ s}$ is $60\text{ m}$.
